## Responses are organized as follows:
## **#1)** raised point
**>>>** response and explanation to reviewer

## **### Reviewer #1:**

**#1.1)** This paper presents two cryo-EM structures of heart-derived AL amyloid (AL59): in a bent and a straight conformation. In addition, and surprisingly, the authors show that many of the amyloid fibrils are intertwined with what is proposed to be collagen-VI. The latter observation is supported by the cryo-EM images, including a sub-nanometer resolution reconstruction of the half-bead volume, as well as by mass-spectrometry data and immuno-EM labelling. In particular, the observation that COLVI may form filaments together with the amyloid is interesting and novel.
**>>>** We thank the reviewer for this overall positive evaluation of our study.

**#1.2)** However, prior to publication, the reconstructions of the two amyloid filament types need to be improved. Reported resolutions are around 4A, which is insufficient for reliable atomic modelling (as explained in reference 44). Therefore, the risk of errors in the proposed atomic models is too large. Even though the disulfide bond may provide some handle on tracing the main chain, hardly any side chain densities are visible in Fig 2a. The authors even acknowledge in the main text that part of their

atomic model is uncertain. The solution is relatively straightforward. As (small-ish) data sets were collected on a 200kV microscope on a Falcon3 detector, collecting new data on a 300kV microscope, possibly with a K3 or a Falcon4 detector would easily extend the resolution to that required for reliable atomic modelling.

**>>>** Firstly, the suggested solution is not as straightforward as the reviewer may assume. Unfortunately we do not have any of the _ex vivo_ amyloid sample left to collect additional datasets. However, to address the concerns of the reviewer, we have re-analyzed the dataset applying two major changes to the reconstruction protocol: (i) changing the number of unique asymmetrical units from six to three, thereby increasing the number of extracted particles to 240k (ii) adding and fine-tuning the tau_fudge regularization parameter during 3D auto-refinement.

Applying these changes, we have reconstructed the straight structure to a resolution of 3.6 Å, based on the fourier shell correlation between the two half-maps at a threshold value of 0.143 (FSC0.143). In the new version of the manuscript, we have highlighted this reconstruction as our main or reference structure. The map features continuous density for the backbone of the entire model, and shows clear density to place confidently the disulfide-bond between residues Cys-22 and Cys-87. Furthermore, glycosylation is not only indicated by additional density around the side-chain of Asn-19, but also confirmed by mass spectrometry. These features of the density allowed us to model the straight structure with high confidence. We want to emphasize that the new model is virtually identical to the model that we have built previously into the map with lower FSC-based resolution estimate. Since the two other reconstructions have lower resolutions (3.9 Å), we have toned down our interpretation of these structures.

Thus, we believe that the new reconstruction of the ‘straight’ structure fulfills the main criteria highlighted in ref. 44: the reconstruction (i) is closer to 3.5 Å, thus beyond the critical 4 Å resolution limit (ii) features continuous main-chain density and (iii) resolves (bulky) side chains convincingly.
This has led to following changes of the text and figures:
- **p. 5 / ll. 92-95:** Here, we report …

- **p. 7– p.8 / ll. 129-169:** entire paragraph entitled " The structure of glycosylated AL59 displays a stable core and two flexible segments adopting alternative conformations” was updated and adjusted to the new reconstructions.
- **p. 18/ ll. 398-413:** Updated materials and methods section.
- **p. 19/ ll. 422-429:** Updated model creation of new structures.
- **p. 22/ ll. 507-509:** New deposition codes.
- **Fig. 2:** Focus on reference ‘straight’ structure.
- **Fig. 3:** Two additional AL59 structures that can be found together with the reference structure on the same fibril.
- **Fig. 4:** Adjusted to new structure.
- **Supplementary Tab. 2**
- **Supplementary Fig. 2-4**
**#1.3)** Fig 2e shows a beta-strand separation of 7.9 and 7.6A. This must be incorrect.
**>>>** Indeed, the reviewer has misinterpreted the figure. The arrow indicates

the distance that a single polypeptide layer traverses along the long axis of the fibril, which has also been referred to as height difference. To make the figure clearer we have now added both the information about the layer separation and the polypeptide
height difference, as described in the figure legend. Therefore we have changed the representation in the new figure version.
- **Fig. 2:** The height difference of the polypeptide layer is indicated for the central layer, highlighted as thick ribbon. The helical rise distance is also shown.

**#1.4)** “If stacked on the same fibril, the terminal segments of the bent and straight structures would clash (Fig. 3a), suggesting that the two classes are unlikely to coexist within one fibril.” The signal along Z is particularly unreliable at the reported resolutions. Also, there could be small imperfections along a single fibril, which could lead to mixed type fibrils (as has been observed for amyloids of other proteins, like TDP-43). Therefore, it would be good to tone down the main text on how mixed-type filaments are unlikely. The existence of a blurry 3D class indicates probably an inability to separate the two types, further suggesting that mixed-type filaments may exist in the data.
**>>>** We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. Indeed, re-processing the

dataset has led to different particle stacks, and our previous conclusion was not confirmed. Indeed, all three structures can co-exist on the same fibril. Furthermore, ~160k particles were not assigned any structure, hampering any conclusion regarding the particle distribution among the tubes.

- **p.8 / ll. 163-165:** All three structures can be found together on the same fibril (Fig. 3c). Additional variants may be present in the ~160k particles that were not assigned any structure (Fig. 3c, d).
**#1.5)** Asn19 density is modelled as a sugar: again the density does not support this modelling.

**>>>** Asn19 clearly displays extra density, and the presence of N- glycosylation was demonstrated by mass spectrometry. Thus, we believe that data are sufficiently sound for building an N-glycosylation in the structure.
**#1.6)** I am not sure how Fig 5b relates to the rest of Fig 5.

**>>>** We thought it helpful for the reader to get an understanding of the current view of how the three COLVI subunits assemble into these remarkable beadon-a-string microfibrils. However, as this part is not critical to follow our manuscript, in keeping with Reviewer’s suggestion we have shifted this part to the supplement.
##  **Supplementary Fig. 5a**

**#1.7)** Fig 5d is not convincing. Why has the contrast of the 2D class average been made so black-white? Please rescale linearly from the smallest value being black to the largest value being white.

**>>>** Indeed, this analysis represents weak additional evidence that we had collected before we have obtained the IEM and cryo-ET data presented in Fig. 6. Given that it is not essential to prove COLVI identity, we have shifted this analysis to the supplement and have also added the 2D class as output by cryoSPARC.
##  **Supplementary Fig. 5c**
**#1.8)** Their maps of the beads is “resembling the available 48 Å resolution map of COLVI extracted from bovine cornea”. This needs to be quantified with an FSC curve between the two maps.
**>>>** In our manuscript we were referring to the overall resemblance of the bead-on-a-string structures, as well as of their half-bead shapes. We have toned down this particular sentence.
- **p. 10-11 / ll. 221-222:** …  with an overall shape reminiscent to that of COLVI from _bovine cornea_[52] .

Furthermore, we have also obtained the COLVI map from the authors and calculated the FSC between the two reconstructions, yielding resolution values of ~35 and ~60 Å at the FSC-thresholds of 0.143 and 0.5, respectively. The map-in-map fitting routine of ChimeraX[1] yielded correlation values of about 0.85 for both hands of the maps. A direct comparison of the 2D classes, 3D reconstructions and corresponding FSC curve is shown here in this response letter on the next page. We believe such comparison is beyond the scope of the manuscript and it is only shown in this letter.
> 1 https://www.cgl.ucsf.edu/chimerax/docs/user/tools/fitmap.html#fitmaps
**==> picture [381 x 232] intentionally omitted <==**

**Figure 1. Comparing the reconstructions of human and bovine COLVI reconstructed in this study and by Godwin and co-worker.** Comparison of the (a) 2D classes and (b) 3D reconstructions. The maps were superimposed in ChimeraX with map-to-map correlation values of ~0.85. Both hands were tested. (c) The FSC between the two maps.
**#1.9)** “We did not construct a molecular model, but found ample space to place 11
VWFA domains in the quarter-bead volume (Supplementary Fig. 6b).” This is meaningless.
**>>>** We have removed this speculative part.
## **### Reviewer #2:**

**#2.1)** This is a very interesting and methodologically well-done study that makes a significant contribution to key questions of AL amyloidosis, such as the structural basis and mechanism of AL fibril formation, factors that contribute to the stabilization of the aggregates, and how AL fibrils interact with components of the extracellular matrix. The manuscript is concise and well-written. There is a good use of technical language. All figures are well-designed and effectively convey information. References cited are appropriate for the manuscript. Only one additional reference is suggested.
Some of the most significant contributions of this study are listed below.

A significant contribution of this study is to reveal the structural bases of the interaction between the AL amyloid fibrils and collagen, a component of the extracellular matrix. This information is relevant not only to our understanding of how AL fibrils relate to matrix components but may also contribute to understanding the effect of extracellular matrix components on the AL fibril assembly mechanism. It may also help understand why it has been so difficult to promote the removal of the AL deposits through antibodies or other approaches that promote macrophagemediated phagocytosis and dissolution of AL fibrils.

Another important finding reported in this manuscript is the evidence of microheterogeneity in the AL fibrils that determines variations of the common structural core. This adds to previous reports that highlight the structural plasticity of AL fibrils. The structural heterogeneity reported in this study may translate into differences in the mechanical properties of the aggregates, impacting the way the fibrils interact with the cell membrane.

One of the most notable findings reported in this manuscript is the similar topology adopted by AL-59 and FOR005 light chains in the amyloid state. Since both proteins belong to the lambda-3 subgroup, this finding suggests that certain structural factors, other than somatic mutations, also contribute to determining the topology of the amyloid fold of AL fibrils. If confirmed in further studies, it may be a starting point for developing the ability to predict light chain amyloid folding based on sequence.

The authors found that in the AL fibril AL59, a fragment of the CL domain extends beyond residue 106, located within the VL-CL binding region. As the authors state, this finding supports the idea that light chain proteolysis in vivo occurs primarily after aggregation. This is a significant contribution to understanding the role of proteolysis in light chain amyloid aggregation, a topic that is still controversial.
**>>>** We thank the reviewer for this overall positive evaluation of our study.

**#2.2)** How the CL fragment associates with the N-terminal segment of the VL in the straight class suggests that the CL is fully or at least partially unfolded into the AL-59 AL fibril. Cooperative unfolding of the VL and CL domains may be a key step in the amyloid aggregation mechanism of some light chains. What do the authors think about this hypothesis?

**>>>** Reviewer 2 raises a very crucial issue. In general, all available structures of LC fibrils do not show any conservation between the native and the fibrillar LC structures, implying a full reorganization of the protein upon aggregation. AL59 is no exception and the interactions between the N-terminal segments of VL and CL domains are unseen in native LCs. In vitro studies typically indicate that LCs unfolding is a one step process and to our best knowledge no data in support of an intermediate state with unfolded VL and folded CL are available. Thus, Reviewer’s is

very plausible: concomitant unfolding of VL and CL domains are necessary for AL59 to form amyloid fibrils. However, given that the cryo-EM structures here presented do not provide direct information on the aggregation process but show only the end state, we refrain from speculating on the molecular steps of AL59 aggregation.

**#2.3)** Introduction, lines 50-51. The statement “Systemic AL amyloidosis is caused by a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people” sounds like AL amyloidosis derives from another disorder, a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with the low mentioned incidence. This is true when you talk about systemic light chain amyloidosis secondary to multiple myeloma. AL amyloidosis is known as primary amyloidosis because it is the primary disorder. I think that the correct statement is “Systemic AL amyloidosis is a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people”.
**>>>** changed in the text.
- **p. 4 / ll. 52-53:** Systemic AL amyloidosis is a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people.
**#2.4)** I noted that the authors used the continuous numbering of the amino acids of

the immunoglobulin light chain. This does not consider insertions in CDR1 and the convention of introducing a gap at position 10 in lambda light chains to allow structural alignment with kappa light chains. The two most widely used immunoglobulin numbering systems are those proposed by Kabat and Chothia and Lesk, respectively. Although these numbering systems differ in the location of insertions in the CDR1 of light chains, they identify highly conserved residues as structural references. Two examples in the VL are Trp35 and the intradomain

disulfide bond between Cys23 and Cys88, respectively. In this manuscript, these are numbered Trp34, Cys22, and Cys88. The use of a structural-based numbering system in immunoglobulins makes it easier to understand studies like the one presented in this manuscript for researchers working in areas where systematic numbering is the rule, such as antibody modeling and X-ray crystallography. Today, the number of cryo-EM structures of AL fibrils is just 5, all of them of lambda type. But in a few years, with many more kappa and lambda cryo-EM structures, if each laboratory uses continuous numbering, some confusion will arise over the identity of topologically equivalent residues. A good review of the significance and implications of antibody numbering is Mathieu Dondelinger et al.(1)

**>>>** The residue numbering of molecular models is indeed a controversial issue, not only with respect to antibody residue numbering. We agree with the reviewer that Kabat (or Chothia) numbering would help the reader to identify important conserved residues more easily. We have therefore added a sentence to the main manuscript and included Supplementary Tab. 3.
- **p. 7 / ll. 141-142:** … bond between residues Cys-22 and Cys-87 (or Cys-23 and Cys-88 according to Kabat numbering of antibodies, see Supplementary Tab. 3), …
##  **Supplementary Tab. 3**

**#2.5)** In 2000, D. L. Harris et al. reported that light chains from patients with AL amyloidosis, but not non-amyloidogenic Bence-Jones proteins, form fibrillar deposits in fibroblast monolayer cell cultures (2). They found evidence that amyloidogenic light chains bind to nascent collagen, an event that promotes light chain misfolding and amyloid aggregation. They observed that light chain amyloid fibrils were

interspersed with nascent collagen in the in vitro system. I suggest citing this study since, to my knowledge, it is the first to provide evidence suggesting a role for the interaction between amyloidogenic light chains and collagen in the aggregation mechanism.

2. Harris DL, King E, Ramsland PA, Edmundson AB. Binding of nascent collagen by amyloidogenic light chains and amyloid fibrillogenesis in monolayers of human fibrocytes. J Mol Recognit. 2000;13(4):198-212.
**>>>** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this interesting study that we
have included as reference #40.
- **p. 34 / ll. 698-700:** added reference
## **### Reviewer #3:**

**#3.1)** In this study the authors present a structural analysis of amyloid fibers extracted from the tissue of a patient with Light Chain Amyloidosis. The key claim of the paper, as I understand it, is that the heart-derived AL59 adopts 3 distinct conformations (2 of which are presented at almost near-atomic resolutions), its fold is similar to that of related LC amyloid fibrils and, most importantly, that AL59 fibrils form a helical superstructure with Collagen VI.
**>>>** The reviewer is absolutely correct, however, another key finding is that we present the first AL amyloid structure with an extended constant domain fragment in its core.
**#3.2.1)** Whereas the hypothesis regarding the potential role of collagen in protecting the amyloids from macrophages is attractive, more evidence is required to support it.

**>>>** As clearly stated in our manuscript, we have not put forward the hypothesis that collagen protects amyloids from macrophages. This hypothesis has been formulated recently by the laboratory of Jonathan Wall (Jackson _et al._ (2022) _Amyloid_ &  Richey (2019) _Am. J. Pathol._ ). However, we believe that this hypothesis is very relevant for the helical superstructure presented in our study.

**#3.2.2)** Most importantly, the whole set of experiments is based on a single extraction procedure from a single patient and might be an artifact of sample handling. Why previous structural works on fibrils from cardiac tissue of AL patients (ref. 3, 15-19) didn’t report similar interactions with collagen, given the LC fibrils adopt similar fold?
**>>>** We have speculated extensively about the raised issue in our manuscript

and refer the reviewer to read carefully lines 270-283 on pages 12-13 of our manuscript. In any case the mode of interaction between amyloid fibrils and COLVI seems to be very unlikely to be formed between non-interacting molecules during an extraction procedure. Conversely Reviewer’s argument may be turned around and we may pose the question whether the currently applied amyloid extraction protocols remove biologically relevant but potentially weakly associated ECM components.
**#3.2.3)** In this context, the very low number of particles used in Fig 5d (78!) is particularly worrying.

**>>>** Indeed, this data represents only weak supporting evidence and has been shifted to the supplementary material in the revised version. The key experiments to demonstrate the concatenation of COLVI with AL59 into helical superstructures are the immuno-electron microscopy (IEM) and cryogenic electron tomography (cryoET) data shown in Fig. 6.
##  **Supplementary Fig. 5c**
**#3.3)** What would be the possible physiological role of various AL59 conformers?

**>>>** The conformers are likely energetically similar and therefore visible. We do not hypothesize these conformers to have a physiological role. To date some degree of structural variability in _ex vivo_ fibrils have been observed in several systems (e.g. AA, ATTR, AL amyloidoses).
**#3.4)** Why the mixed conformation could not be solved to a better resolution given it
was most abundant (27k particles vs 16k and 22k for the other classes)?

**>>>** After re-processing the dataset, these numbers have changed. Indeed, the highest resolution reconstruction comprises the highest number of particles. We refer the reviewer to the following sites:
- **p. 7– p.8 / ll. 129-169:** results section " The structure of glycosylated AL59 displays a stable core and two flexible segments adopting alternative conformations”.
- **p. 18/ ll. 398-413:** Updated materials and methods section.
- **Supplementary Tab. 2**
**#3.5)** Which conformation (bent, straight, mixed) of AL59 is most similar to FOR005?

**>>>** FOR005 aligns mostly with the u-shaped core of AL59 that is virtually identical in all three structures. The superimposition in Fig. 4c shows the straight structure aligned to FOR005. This information has also been added to the manuscript.
 **p. 9/ ll. 178:** … is superimposable on the ‘straight’ AL59 structure …
**#3.6)** Which conformation of AL59 is predominantly collagen-bound?
**>>>** Our analysis showed that about 80% of all fibrils are concatenated with
collagen. Since the three structures co-exist within the same fibril, we assume that collagen binding is not specific to any of the three structures.
**#3.7)** Why RT EM analyses with resin-embedded tissues and post-embedding immunogold staining were not performed? Scarcity of tissue?

All available cardiac tissue has been dedicated to fibril extraction and Cryo-EM/TEM studies, thus frozen without fixation.  However patient tissues were Congo Red positive and amyloids were identified by immuno-electron microscopy; for more details see the "Clinical characteristics of patient AL59" section of Materials and Methods on p. 15 ll. 297-310.

**#3.8)** I believe more work is required to claim that the paper provides ‘the first structural evidence of interactions between amyloid and collagen’ – at the moment it is not clear even at the domain level whether the interaction is specific and what are the molecular basis.

**>>>** We have applied cryo-TEM to determine the _ex vivo_ structure of AL59 amyloid fibrils. Serendipitously we have observed in raw micrographs that a polymer is wrapped around the vast majority of the extracted fibrils. This observation was reproduced in several independent extractions. We obtain a low-resolution reconstruction of helical superstructures between amyloid and the filament that we have identified unambiguously as COLVI by IEM. To our best knowledge, this is the first evidence of an interaction between amyloid and other protein polymers localized in the amyloid plaques. As clearly discussed in the manuscript, our data do not allow a molecular description of the interface or to claim that the interactions between amyloids and COLVI are specific or unspecific. Yet we believe that the data presented in this manuscript fully support the claim that this is ‘the first structural evidence of interactions between amyloid and collagen’.
**#3.9)** Line 39: ‘confirmations’ instead of ‘conformations’
**>>>** amended
## **### Reviewer #4**

**#4.1)** I was unable to find any MS data either in the supplement or a public repository. The list of protein accessions and names in the supplement is not sufficient for evaluation or informing readers. I expect to be able to view peptide and PSM-level data in supplement or repository. Peptide level information is necessary to assess the confidence in the identification and for informing structural information that can be informed based on the peptides identified. Especially as the authors claim that PNGase F digestion was used to identify sites of previous glycosylation, this needs to be supported by high resolution and high mass accuracy MS and MS/MS. Also, to avoid over-interpretation of spontaneous deamidation, experiments that analyze the proteins after trypsin digestion but without PNGase F are important and I did not see that. While I see the cartoon representation in Supplementary Figure 1, I need to see the peptide information (sequence, m/z, error, missed cleavages, etc)

**>>>** To meet Reviewer’s request we have deposited the MS data in the PRIDE database. The reviewer can access the two depositions with following parameters: PXD049369 (Username: reviewer_pxd049369@ebi.ac.uk; Password: PAvjLRIY) and PXD049301 (Username: reviewer_pxd049301@ebi.ac.uk; Password: LJ67h8mF). We have also added additional information in Supplementary Tab. 4.

N-glycosylation site was evaluated indirectly, by comparison between semi-tryptic peptides detected in deglycosylated samples, digested with PNGase F, and in control samples, where enzyme was replaced by water. We have implemented the method

section with details to better explain this procedure. All spectra attributed to peptides supposed to be deamidated by PNGase F were manually checked. Peptides containing deamidated Asp19 are detected in the digested sample, while they are not observed in the undigested sample. Furthermore, in terms of deamidation occurrences, differences were not found in other Asparagine residues, where a spontaneous modification may occur during sample preparation. We added two supplementary tables containing AL59 peptides list and relative information for sample digested and undigested with PNGase F.

## **Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):**

The revised version of this paper has improved to some extent. However, access to the maps and models reveals that the reconstructions for the bent and mixed conformations are not of sufficient quality to support the conclusions drawn in the paper. Although the reported resolution of these maps is claimed to be 3.9A, there are many false connections, additional densities, and missing densities for the modelled main-chain in both reconstructions. The data bases should not be polluted with these suboptimal maps and models. Therefore, before acceptance of this paper, I would suggest removing all mentions of the bent and mixed conformations from the paper. This would take nothing away from the main conclusions and prevent the authors from making mistakes.

I would also suggest using the typical XY-view, which shows the sum of five consecutive cross-section slices in a linear greyscale, where black corresponding to the minimum and white to the maximum density value for Figure 2. The current blue map representations in Figure 2 and Suppl Fig 4 hides suboptimal features in the maps. I attach an image with such XY-views of the straight (left) and bent (right) reconstructions. These images show the ok-ish quality of the straight conformation
(although the density at the termini is getting worse) and the suboptimal quality of the bent conformation (with the evidence for the supposedly bending termini being extremely weak).
**>>>** We have removed the two additional structures as requested. Specifically, we have removed entirely
- Fig. 3, displaying the two additional ‘bent’ and ‘mixed’ structures
- Supplemental Fig. 4, displaying their maps and models
- the structural parameters from Supplementary Tab. 2.
and associated references in the text.

However, we emphasize that two members of our group, V. Speranzini and M. Milazzo, have processed the same dataset applying slightly different parameters/workflows to obtain these two additional structures at different stages during the reconstruction process. While the reconstructions are of lower quality and worse resolution, they are present in the dataset. Our structural data solidly show that AL59 exhibits structural heterogeneity. Our finding is added to accumulating evidence that amyloid fibrils can have structural breaks. Therefore, we should communicate, and not hide, our findings to the scientific community. Acknowledging the limitations of the reconstructions, we have added linear greyscale XY slices of these reconstructions to Fig. 2d. Furthermore, we have deposited the dataset at EMPIAR, and we are certain that other scientists re-processing the same dataset would come to similar conclusions.

## Helical superstructures between amyloid and collagen in cardiac fibrils from a patient with AL amyloidosis 

Received: 17 November 2023 Accepted: 18 July 2024 Check for updates 

Tim Schulte[1,2,12] , Antonio Chaves-Sanjuan 3,12, Valentina Speranzini3,12, Kevin Sicking[4,5] , Melissa Milazzo 3, Giulia Mazzini 6, Paola Rognoni 6, Serena Caminito 6, Paolo Milani 6, Chiara Marabelli 3, Alessandro Corbelli7, Luisa Diomede 7, Fabio Fiordaliso 7, Luigi Anastasia 1,8, Carlo Pappone 1,8,9, Giampaolo Merlini 6, Martino Bolognesi 3, Mario Nuvolone 6, Rubén Fernández-Busnadiego 4,5,10,11, Giovanni Palladini6 & Stefano Ricagno 1,3 

Systemic light chain (LC) amyloidosis (AL) is a disease where organs are damaged by an overload of a misfolded patient-specific antibody-derived LC, secreted by an abnormal B cell clone. The high LC concentration in the blood leads to amyloid deposition at organ sites. Indeed, cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has revealed unique amyloid folds for heart-derived fibrils taken from different patients. Here, we present the cryo-EM structure of heartderived AL amyloid (AL59) from another patient with severe cardiac involvement. The double-layered structure displays a u-shaped core that is closed by a β-arc lid and extended by a straight tail. Noteworthy, the fibril harbours an extended constant domain fragment, thus ruling out the variable domain as sole amyloid building block. Surprisingly, the fibrils were abundantly concatenated with a proteinaceous polymer, here identified as collagen VI (COLVI) by immuno-electron microscopy (IEM) and mass-spectrometry.

Cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET) showed how COLVI wraps around the amyloid forming a helical superstructure, likely stabilizing and protecting the fibrils from clearance. Thus, here we report structural evidence of interactions between amyloid and collagen, potentially signifying a distinct pathophysiological mechanism of amyloid deposits. 

Systemic AL amyloidosis is a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people[1] . AL amyloidosis is due to the overexpression of an amyloidogenic LC that misfolds and forms amyloid deposits in several organs[2] . The circulating LC molecules exert proteotoxicity which concurs with the mass effect produced by amyloid deposits to fatal organ dysfunction[1] . Due to genomic recombination and somatic mutations every AL patient bears a virtually unique amyloidogenic LC sequence, originating from either the λ− or κ−gene locus[3][,][4] . Most patients areaffected by deposits in multiple 

organs, but heart manifestation dictates the prognosis in ~75% of cases[5][–][9] . Without its associated heavy chain, free LCs fold into homodimers where each monomer consists of an N-terminal variable domain (VL) and a C-terminal constant domain (CL) connected by a flexible joining region[10][–][13] . While free LCs are eliminated rapidly under healthy conditions, abnormal levels of an amyloidogenic LC cause vast accumulations of cross-β amyloid fibrils in AL amyloidosis[1][,][14] . ## Results & discussion 

## Ex vivo AL59 amyloids form abundant complexes with copurified unknown polymer 

AL59 amyloids were extracted from the heart apex tissue of a 56 years old woman, who had died from progressive heart failure and systemic AL amyloidosis (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Tab. 1). The amyloid extraction procedure is standardised in our laboratory as previously described[16][,][28][,][44] .

AL59 belongs to the λ3 light chain family, and is more specifically encoded by the variable gene IGLV3-01, and IGLJ2*01 for the joining segment. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) carried out on extracted fibrils revealed peptide fragments corresponding to residue numbers 1-204 of AL59 (Supplementary Fig. 1). To determine the molecular structure of AL59 amyloids, cryo-EM data were collected. Inspection of raw cryo-EM micrographs of the vitrified amyloid extract revealed fibrils with an alternating width pattern, from which we estimated a crossover length of ~1200 Å (Fig. 1a). Surprisingly, an additional polymer distinct from amyloid was abundantly present in all fibril samples extracted from AL59 cardiac tissue (Fig. 1a). This polymer was present both in isolated form and also AL59-associated. In its unbound form, the polymer exhibits a bipartite repeating structure comprising 500 Å long beads connected by 600 Å long and 50 Å thin fibres, thus exhibiting a periodicity of 1100 Å (Fig. 1a). With further micrograph inspection, we also recognised the same bead-like shape as part of the amyloid-decorating polymer (Fig. 1a). Among 184 micrographs with higher visual contrast, we found the polymer decorating about 80% of amyloid fibrils. To unveil the structural properties of this unique AL59/polymer complex, we also collected cryo-ET data. In agreement with the cryo-EM micrographs, tomograms revealed undecorated amyloid, free polymer, as well as abundant polymer-decorated amyloid (Fig. 1b).

## The structure of glycosylated AL59 is double-layered and adopts a u-shaped core that is closed by a β-arc segment and extended by a straight tail 

To determine the structure of AL59, free and polymer-decorated amyloids were picked as single population for standard helical reconstruction[45][,][46] . A reference-free 2D class average of particles extracted with a box size of ~1600 Å confirmed the estimated crossover length of ~1200 Å (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Class averages of particles extracted with a smaller box size of 302 Å, revealed the amyloid-characteristic β-spine (Supplementary Fig. 2b). The 2D class averages were characteristic of amyloid, lacking any features attributable to the abundant polymer. 

From the initially extracted ~240 k particles, ~38 k were reconstructed to a final map with a resolution of 3.6 Å (Fig. 2a). Based on the AL59 amino acid sequence, we built the entire structure unambiguously into the continuous density, starting from the disulphide bond between residues Cys-22 and Cys-87 (or Cys-23 and Cys-88 according to Kabat numbering of antibodies, see Supplementary Tab. 3), clearly marked in the map (Fig. 2a). The single proto-filament of the built model comprises residues 1-118, 51 of which form 9 β-strands (Fig. 2b).

## AL59 adopts a fold related to λ3-FOR005, but harbours an extended constant domain fragment in its amyloid core 

In keeping with the four other reported ex vivo LC amyloid structures (Fig. 3a)[3][,][15][–][19] , AL59 adopts a fold substantially different from its native structure (Fig. 3b), but retains the conserved disulphide bond between Cys-22 and Cys-87. The 59-64% sequence-identical VL-domains of the λ1- and λ6-subfamily members (Fig. 3a) adopt amyloid folds different from AL59. Interestingly, the structure of the ~70% sequence-identical and non-glycosylated λ3-FOR005 is superimposable on the AL59 structure with a root mean square deviation of ~4 Å over 81 aligned residues (Fig. 3a, c).

The two related folds exhibit similar positioning of the disulphide bond and CDR segments (Fig. 3c). Glycosylation does not seem to impact this specific amyloid fold. In contrast, the authors of a previous study suggested that glycosylation of λ1-FOR001 contributes to define its specific amyloid fold[18] . Thus, here we show that two LCs belonging to the same germline subfamily, but from different individuals, adopt a related amyloid fold. This observation corroborates our previous findings of identical structure of fibrils extracted from different organs of the same individual, indicating that the fibril fold is dictated by its primary sequence[19] . 

In contrast to the previously reported LC amyloid structures[3][,][15][–][19] , AL59 is to the best of our knowledge the first structure with a CL domain fragment extending beyond residue position 106, that is located within the VL-CL joining region. A model for LC amyloid aggregation posits that proteolytic cleavage of the joining region is required to trigger fibril formation by the amyloidogenic VL domain molecules[48][,][49] . Evidently, such a model cannot be applied to AL59 amyloid aggregation. If a proteolytic event is necessary to destabilise AL59 native fold, it may occur in the CL domain. Furthermore, we applied our established LC-MS/MS protocol which revealed proteolysis hotspots in the CL domain of AL59 (Fig. 3b), similarly to those reported for λ6-AL55 and λ1-H7[28][,][44] . These observations support our previous interpretation that in vivo proteolysis occurs mostly post aggregation[28][,][44] . 

Thus, λ3-AL59 amyloid adopts a fold related to LC fibrils derived from the same germline subfamily, regardless of originating from a different patient.

The inclusion of an extended CL-derived fragment in the AL59 amyloid core, combined with the extensive fragmentation of the CL domain, point at the CL domain as main target for in vivo proteolysis.

Generally, the rigid AL59 fibrils were better defined than the heterogeneous COLVI decorating density. Thus, although we observed beadlike structures in amyloid-associated COLVI (Fig. 1b), our attempts to average sub-tomograms were not successful, preventing a molecular reconstruction of the AL59-COLVI complex. Notably, COLVI wraps around the central AL59 fibril, adopting the helical twist and rise values of the amyloid but with a three times larger helical radius (Fig. 5b). While COLVI adopts a non-helical superstructure on its own, the amyloid fibril imprints its helical structure on COLVI, resulting in complexes with an interaction interface spanning for thousands of angstrom. Such a chirality transfer is regarded as fundamental mechanism across scales in natural and artificial systems[59][–][62] . Specifically amyloids, exploited in nanotechnology and biotechnology, were reported as chirality inducers[60][,][63][,][64] . 

Recently, collagen was reported to play a protective role against amyloid clearance by macrophages[34][,][35] . The helical superstructures between AL59 and COLVI with such extensive interaction surfaces can exemplify how collagen may contribute to amyloid stabilisation and may hide misfolded aggregates from macrophage activity[34][,][35] . Earlier studies have also demonstrated adverse effects of collagen in various other amyloidoses. In dialysis-related Aβ2 M amyloidosis, collagen facilitates β2 m aggregation and interacts weakly with mature β2 m fibrils[36][–][39] . In ATTR amyloidosis, transthyretin (TTR) tends to aggregate in the presence of basement membrane components such as collagen 

IV, whose expression correlates with amyloid accumulation[65][,][66] .

Collagen levels are also increased in the brains of Alzheimer’s patients where collagen seems to play a neuroprotective role and facilitates the formation of mature Aβ fibrils[41][–][43][,][67] . Then why had no structural evidence of such interactions been reported to date? A possible answer is that these interactions are typically weak and do not withstand the forces exerted during extraction. The unexpected abundance of COLVI in our micrographs may be related to unique amyloid features. LC fibrils in different AL patients present distinct surface residues, thus forming intermolecular complexes with variable stability. By serendipity, AL59 amyloids can interact strongly with COLVI, resulting in the abundant and reproducible observation of the AL59/COLVI complex in our ex vivo extracts. Moreover mild extraction protocols may facilitate the observation of such complexes. Remarkably, a micrograph of λ3-FOR005, shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 of that study[15] , displays an amyloidconcatenated polymer resembling COLVI. Thus, the concatenation of amyloid with collagen, exemplified here as helical superstructures, may represent a general mechanism by which collagen(s) could modify the recognition of amyloid by host defence mechanisms. 

In summary, here we report the cryo-EM structure of AL59 amyloids extracted from an AL patient with severe cardiac involvement. Glycosylated λ3-AL59 adopts a double-layered structure featuring a u-shaped core with a β-arc lid and a straight tail extension. AL59 is to the best of our knowledge the first LC amyloid structure comprising a CL domain fragment, thus incompatible with the model suggesting that LC amyloids are formed by isolated VL domains released upon LC proteolysis.

Surprisingly, AL59 fibrils form helical superstructures with COLVI, representing evidence of a stable interaction between amyloid and ECM components. This observation provides insights about the potential role of collagen as a modulating agent of amyloid deposits, potentially signifying a distinct pathophysiological mechanism for amyloidoses.

A single reference-free 2D class average was used for initial model generation following published protocols[45] , by applying an estimated crossover distance of 1200 Å (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Extraction of short segments with a 340 pixel box-size and inter-box distance of 15 Å yielded 240,985 segments. Reference-free 2D classes obtained with a regularisation value of T = 8 yielded averages with clearly visible cross-β structure (Supplemental Fig. 2b). The initial model was re-scaled and re-windowed to match the un-binned short segments and low-pass-filtered to 10 Å. 

Initial 3D auto-refinement applying C1 symmetry as well as helical twist and rise values of −0.7° and 4.9 Å, respectively, yielded a 4.2 Å resolution map. Initial 3D classification with a regularisation value of T = 24 yielded two structural classes comprising 54,825 (55k) and 31,113 (31k) particles, each displaying polypeptide features.

3D classification of the 55k particle-set showed two structures comprising 37,904 (38k) and 16,921 (17k) particles, respectively. The structure presented herein was reconstructed from the 38k particle-set by 3D auto-refinement applying a 5 Å low-pass filtered reference map, 270 Å mask, helical tube radius of 180 Å and Z-value of 30%. Post-processing with a B-factor of −106 Å[2] yielded a 3.6 Å resolution map, assessed using the 0.143 FSC threshold criterion (Supplementary Tab. 2). The two additional structures emerged early and late during reconstruction of the main structure. The early-emerging structure was reconstructed from 23,010 particles, selected by 3D classification of the initial 31k particle set. The late-emerging structure was reconstructed from 12,355 particles, selected by 3D classification of the later obtained 17k particle set. Both structures were 3D auto-refined using the same settings as for the main structure, and post-processed to yield 3.9 Å resolution maps. 

Model building of AL59. The initial model was built de novo in Coot[73] , starting from the position of the disulphide bond between Cys-22 and Cys-87. The polypeptide backbone of the model was extended by placement of poly-Alanine residues into the continuous map. Considering bulky side-chain features, residues were mutated to match the AL59 protein sequence. The model was iteratively built and refined in Coot, Chimera-Isolde and Phenix real-space refinement with reference-model restraints[73][–][76] . The additional density around Asn-19 was modelled as N-linked N-acetyl glucosamine (NAG), representing the first building block of the common N-glycan core[77] .

The final model comprising five 118-residue long chains in each proto-filament was obtained by refinement with additional non-crystallographic symmetry (NCS) restraints. Molprobity score and EMDB[78][,][79] atom inclusion values of 1.56 and 0.74, respectively, suggest a physically valid model with good map support.

## Reporting summary 

Immuno-electron microscopy (IEM).

10 µl drop of the AL59 extract were placed at room temperature for 30 min on a 200 mesh formvar/ carbon coated nichel grid (EMS, Hatfield, PA, USA). After absorbing the excess of the suspension with Whatman filter paper, fibrils were then incubated with a rabbit anti-human collagen VI (1:10, Fitzgerald Industries International) overnight at 4 °C in a wet chamber, followed by a donkey anti-rabbit antibody conjugated to a 12 nm colloidal gold (1:75, Jackson Immunoresearch) in block solution for 45 min at 37°. After post-fixation with 2% glutaraldehyde, grids were finally negatively counterstained with 2% uranyl acetate and observed with an Energy Filter Transmission Electron Microscope (EFTEM, ZEISS LIBRA® 120) equipped with YAG scintillator slow scan CCD camera (Sharp eye, TRS, Moorenweis, Germany). 

Cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET). Samples were prepared in the same way as for cryo-EM. Vitrified specimens were imaged on a Titan Krios cryo-transmission electron microscope equipped with a Selectris energy filter with a slit width of 15 eV and a Falcon IV direct electro detector (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Multiple tilt series with a pixel size of 2.32 Å were recorded over a tilt range of −54 to 54 degrees in 3-degree steps with a dose-symmetric scheme using SerialEM and PACE-tomo 1.2[82][,][83] . The total electron dose was kept under 120 electrons/Å². Frames were aligned using MotionCor2 1.5.0[72] . Final tilt series were aligned using fiducial-less patch tracking, down sampled four times, and reconstructed into tomograms by back projection within IMOD 4.11.15[84] . Contrast was enhanced by filtering the tomograms using CTF Deconvolve of isonet 0.2[85] .

reviewer_spans.text: ## Reviewer #1:
Remarks to the Author:

This paper presents two cryo-EM structures of heart-derived AL amyloid (AL59): in a bent and a straight conformation. In addition, and surprisingly, the authors show that many of the amyloid fibrils are intertwined with what is proposed to be collagen-VI. The latter observation is supported by the cryo-EM images, including a sub-nanometer resolution reconstruction of the half-bead volume, as well as by mass-spectrometry data and immuno-EM labelling. In particular, the observation that COLVI may form filaments together with the amyloid is interesting and novel.

However, prior to publication, the reconstructions of the two amyloid filament types need to be improved. Reported resolutions are around 4A, which is insufficient for reliable atomic modelling (as explained in reference 44). Therefore, the risk of errors in the proposed atomic models is too large. Even though the disulfide bond may provide some handle on tracing the main chain, hardly any side chain densities are visible in Fig 2a. The authors even acknowledge in the main text that part of their atomic model is uncertain.

The solution is relatively straightforward. As (small-ish) data sets were collected on a 200kV microscope on a Falcon3 detector, collecting new data on a 300kV microscope, possibly with a K3 or a Falcon4 detector would easily extend the resolution to that required for reliable atomic modelling.
Other comments that need addressing:
Fig 2e shows a beta-strand separation of 7.9 and 7.6A. This must be incorrect.

“If stacked on the same fibril, the terminal segments of the bent and straight structures would clash (Fig. 3a), suggesting that the two classes are unlikely to coexist within one fibril.” The signal along Z is particularly unreliable at the reported resolutions. Also, there could be small imperfections along a single fibril, which could lead to mixed type fibrils (as has been observed for amyloids of other proteins, like TDP-43). Therefore, it would be good to tone down the main text on how mixed-type filaments are unlikely. The existence of a blurry 3D class indicates probably an inability to separate the two types, further suggesting that mixed-type filaments may exist in the data.
Asn19 density is modelled as a sugar: again the reconstructed map is of , the density does not support this modelling.

I am not sure how Fig 5b relates to the rest of Fig 5. Fig 5d is not convincing. Why has the contrast of the 2D class average been made so black-white? Please rescale linearly from the smallest value being black to the largest value being white.
Their maps of the beads is “resembling the available 48 Å resolution map of COLVI extracted from bovine cornea”. This needs to be quantified with an FSC curve between the two maps.
“We did not construct a molecular model, but found ample space to place 11 VWFA domains in the quarter-bead volume (Supplementary Fig. 6b).” This is meaningless.
## Reviewer #2:
Remarks to the Author:
This is a very interesting and methodologically well-done study that makes a significant contribution to key questions of AL amyloidosis, such as the structural basis and mechanism of AL

fibril formation, factors that contribute to the stabilization of the aggregates, and how AL fibrils interact with components of the extracellular matrix. The manuscript is concise and well-written. There is a good use of technical language. All figures are well-designed and effectively convey information. References cited are appropriate for the manuscript. Only one additional reference is suggested.
Some of the most significant contributions of this study are listed below.

A significant contribution of this study is to reveal the structural bases of the interaction between the AL amyloid fibrils and collagen, a component of the extracellular matrix. This information is relevant not only to our understanding of how AL fibrils relate to matrix components but may also contribute to understanding the effect of extracellular matrix components on the AL fibril assembly mechanism. It may also help understand why it has been so difficult to promote the removal of the AL deposits through antibodies or other approaches that promote macrophage-mediated phagocytosis and dissolution of AL fibrils.

Another important finding reported in this manuscript is the evidence of microheterogeneity in the AL fibrils that determines variations of the common structural core. This adds to previous reports that highlight the structural plasticity of AL fibrils. The structural heterogeneity reported in this study may translate into differences in the mechanical properties of the aggregates, impacting the way the fibrils interact with the cell membrane.

One of the most notable findings reported in this manuscript is the similar topology adopted by AL59 and FOR005 light chains in the amyloid state. Since both proteins belong to the lambda-3 subgroup, this finding suggests that certain structural factors, other than somatic mutations, also contribute to determining the topology of the amyloid fold of AL fibrils. If confirmed in further studies, it may be a starting point for developing the ability to predict light chain amyloid folding based on sequence.

The authors found that in the AL fibril AL59, a fragment of the CL domain extends beyond residue 106, located within the VL-CL binding region. As the authors state, this finding supports the idea that light chain proteolysis in vivo occurs primarily after aggregation. This is a significant contribution to understanding the role of proteolysis in light chain amyloid aggregation, a topic that is still controversial.

How the CL fragment associates with the N-terminal segment of the VL in the straight class suggests that the CL is fully or at least partially unfolded into the AL-59 AL fibril. Cooperative unfolding of the VL and CL domains may be a key step in the amyloid aggregation mechanism of some light chains. What do the authors think about this hypothesis? Minor issues

1. Introduction, lines 50-51. The statement “Systemic AL amyloidosis is caused by a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people” sounds like AL amyloidosis derives from another disorder, a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with the low mentioned incidence. This is true when you talk about systemic light chain amyloidosis secondary to multiple myeloma. AL amyloidosis is known as primary amyloidosis because it is the primary disorder. I think that the correct statement is “Systemic AL amyloidosis is a rare plasma cell dyscrasia with an annual incidence of about 12-15 new cases per million people”.

2. I noted that the authors used the continuous numbering of the amino acids of the immunoglobulin light chain. This does not consider insertions in CDR1 and the convention of introducing a gap at position 10 in lambda light chains to allow structural alignment with kappa light chains. The two most widely used immunoglobulin numbering systems are those proposed by Kabat and Chothia and Lesk, respectively. Although these numbering systems differ in the location of insertions in the CDR1 of light chains, they identify highly conserved residues as structural references. Two examples in the VL are Trp35 and the intradomain disulfide bond between Cys23 and Cys88, respectively. In this manuscript, these are numbered Trp34, Cys22, and Cys88. The use of a structural-based numbering system in immunoglobulins makes it easier to understand studies like the one presented in this manuscript for researchers working in areas where systematic numbering is the rule, such as antibody modeling and X-ray crystallography. Today, the number of cryo-EM structures of AL fibrils is just 5, all of them of lambda type. But in a few years, with many more kappa and lambda cryo-EM structures, if each laboratory uses continuous numbering, some confusion will arise over the identity of topologically equivalent residues. A good

review of the significance and implications of antibody numbering is Mathieu Dondelinger et al.(1) 3. In 2000, D. L. Harris et al. reported that light chains from patients with AL amyloidosis, but not non-amyloidogenic Bence-Jones proteins, form fibrillar deposits in fibroblast monolayer cell cultures(2). They found evidence that amyloidogenic light chains bind to nascent collagen, an event that promotes light chain misfolding and amyloid aggregation. They observed that light chain amyloid fibrils were interspersed with nascent collagen in the in vitro system. I suggest citing this study since, to my knowledge, it is the first to provide evidence suggesting a role for the interaction between amyloidogenic light chains and collagen in the aggregation mechanism.

1. Dondelinger M, Filee P, Sauvage E, Quinting B, Muyldermans S, Galleni M, et al. Understanding the Significance and Implications of Antibody Numbering and Antigen-Binding Surface/Residue Definition. Front Immunol. 2018;9:2278.

2. Harris DL, King E, Ramsland PA, Edmundson AB. Binding of nascent collagen by amyloidogenic light chains and amyloid fibrillogenesis in monolayers of human fibrocytes. J Mol Recognit. 2000;13(4):198-212.
## Reviewer #3:
## Remarks to the Author:

In this study the authors present a structural analysis of amyloid fibers extracted from the tissue of a patient with Light Chain Amyloidosis. The key claim of the paper, as I understand it, is that the heart-derived AL59 adopts 3 distinct conformations (2 of which are presented at almost nearatomic resolutions), its fold is similar to that of related LC amyloid fibrils and, most importantly, that AL59 fibrils form a helical superstructure with Collagen VI. Whereas the hypothesis regarding the potential role of collagen in protecting the amyloids from macrophages is attractive, more evidence is required to support it. Most importantly, the whole set of experiments is based on a single extraction procedure from a single patient and might be an artifact of sample handling. Why previous structural works on fibrils from cardiac tissue of AL patients (ref. 3, 15-19) didn’t report similar interactions with collagen, given the LC fibrils adopt similar fold? In this context, the very low number of particles used in Fig 5d (78!) is particularly worrying. Furthermore, a few other points should be addressed:
- What would be the possible physiological role of various AL59 conformers?
- Why the mixed conformation could not be solved to a better resolution given it was most abundant (27k particles vs 16k and 22k for the other classes)?
- Which conformation (bent, straight, mixed) of AL59 is most similar to FOR005?
- Which conformation of AL59 is predominantly collagen-bound?
- Why RT EM analyses with resin-embedded tissues and post-embedding immunogold staining were not performed? Scarcity of tissue?

- I believe more work is required to claim that the paper provides ‘the first structural evidence of interactions between amyloid and collagen’ – at the moment it is not clear even at the domain level whether the interaction is specific and what are the molecular basis.
## Minor issues:
- Line 39: ‘confirmations’ instead of ‘conformations’
## Reviewer #4:
## Remarks to the Author:

I was unable to find any MS data either in the supplement or a public repository. The list of protein accessions and names in the supplement is not sufficient for evaluation or informing readers. I expect to be able to view peptide and PSM-level data in supplement or repository. Peptide level information is necessary to assess the confidence in the identification and for informing structural information that can be informed based on the peptides identified. Especially as the authors claim that PNGase F digestion was used to identify sites of previous glycosylation, this needs to be

supported by high resolution and high mass accuracy MS and MS/MS. Also, to avoid overinterpretation of spontaneous deamidation, experiments that analyze the proteins after trypsin digestion but without PNGase F are important and I did not see that. While I see the cartoon representation in Supplementary Figure 1, I need to see the peptide information (sequence, m/z, error, missed cleavages, etc)
## Reviewer #1:
## Remarks to the Author:

The revised version of this paper has improved to some extent. However, access to the maps and models reveals that the reconstructions for the bent and mixed conformations are not of sufficient quality to support the conclusions drawn in the paper. Although the reported resolution of these maps is claimed to be 3.9A, there are many false connections, additional densities, and missing densities for the modelled main-chain in both reconstructions. The data bases should not be polluted with these suboptimal maps and models. Therefore, before acceptance of this paper, I would suggest removing all mentions of the bent and mixed conformations from the paper. This would take nothing away from the main conclusions and prevent the authors from making mistakes.

I would also suggest using the typical XY-view, which shows the sum of five consecutive crosssection slices in a linear greyscale, where black corresponding to the minimum and white to the maximum density value for Figure 2. The current blue map representations in Figure 2 and Suppl Fig 4 hides suboptimal features in the maps. I attach an image with such XY-views of the straight (left) and bent (right) reconstructions. These images show the ok-ish quality of the straight conformation (although the density at the termini is getting worse) and the suboptimal quality of the bent conformation (with the evidence for the supposedly bending termini being extremely weak).
